blockMcqs.question: Why is a slow node so hard to handle in distributed systems?
options: It corrupts data on disk
It looks identical to a crashed node
It always triggers a split-brain
It forces an immediate leader election
blockMcqs.explanation: With no reply before your timeout, slow and dead are indistinguishable from outside.

blockMcqs.question: Which is NOT a required property of consensus?
options: Agreement: all deciders pick the same value
Validity: the value was proposed
Termination: nodes eventually decide
Locality: each node decides alone
blockMcqs.explanation: Consensus is inherently collective; agreement, validity, and termination define it.

blockMcqs.question: In Raft, what triggers a follower to become a candidate?
options: A client write arrives directly
No heartbeat before its randomized timeout
Its log grows past a fixed size
A majority of peers crash
blockMcqs.explanation: Missing heartbeats suggest a dead leader, so the follower bumps the term and seeks votes.

blockMcqs.question: Why can a new Raft leader never miss a committed entry?
options: All nodes ack before any commit
Any two majorities share at least one node
Leaders copy the whole log on election
Committed entries are written to disk twice
blockMcqs.explanation: Majority overlap plus the up-to-date vote rule guarantees the winner holds committed entries.

blockMcqs.question: In a 3-node Raft cluster, when does a write commit?
options: After all three nodes ack
After the leader writes locally
Once a majority (2 of 3) have it durably
After the next heartbeat round
blockMcqs.explanation: A majority ack suffices, so one slow or dead follower never blocks the write.

blockMcqs.question: How do real systems escape the FLP impossibility result?
options: By synchronizing all clocks perfectly
By adding timeouts and accepting possible stalls
By requiring every node to ack
By giving up safety during partitions
blockMcqs.explanation: Timeouts act as a weak failure detector; safety stays, liveness may pause under bad partitions.

blockMcqs.question: What can vector clocks do that Lamport clocks cannot?
options: Guarantee a total order of events
Detect that two events are concurrent
Use less storage per event
Synchronize wall-clock time
blockMcqs.explanation: When neither vector dominates the other, the events had no causal link.

blockMcqs.question: With N=3 replicas, which R/W pair guarantees reads see the latest write?
options: R=1, W=1 with gossip
blockMcqs.explanation: R + W > N forces read and write sets to overlap; 2 + 2 > 3, but 1 + 2 is not.

blockMcqs.question: What does CAP force you to choose during a network partition?
options: Between latency and throughput
Between consistency and availability
Between leader and follower reads
Between gossip and quorums
blockMcqs.explanation: Only during a partition; otherwise you really trade latency against consistency.

blockMcqs.question: Why are consensus clusters sized odd (3, 5, 7)?
options: Odd counts halve write latency
An even size tolerates no extra failure but adds latency
Majority is undefined for odd sizes
Gossip requires an odd peer count
blockMcqs.explanation: N=4 still tolerates only one failure like N=3, so the extra voter only slows writes.

blockMcqs.question: Why is two-phase commit called a blocking protocol?
options: It needs every node to vote NO
Participants hold locks if the coordinator dies mid-decision
It blocks all reads during the prepare phase
It cannot run across more than two databases
blockMcqs.explanation: After voting YES, a participant can't safely decide alone, so it waits with locks held.
